title: How to practice my solo

kid.t: Warm up first. Never stretch cold.
Watch one 8-count of Hannah's video first, then pause and do it.
Give each part a fun name. Say it out loud while you dance.
Slow first, then with the real music, then full out.
Quiz yourself: no video, no mirror. Then check what you missed.
Always finish from the top, so no part gets forgotten.
Copy the little things from day one: arms, feet, eyes, knees over toes.
Say the counts out loud. When you know it, listen for the music instead.
Watch your clip with a grown-up, then fix just ONE thing.
Before you dance: stand in your first pose, play the song, picture the stage.
No flips without a teacher and a mat. Sleep 9–12 hours.

grown.t: Break the solo into small named chunks.
grown.note: Group steps that belong together and name them; complex skills are learned better when the load is cut down.

grown.t: Watch the phrase on the video before trying it.
grown.note: Dance students who watched first recalled phrases better 10–13 days later than verbal-first learners.

grown.t: Put words to the moves (names, pictures, self-talk).
grown.note: Metaphor names helped 5–6-year-olds remember dance sequences; self-talk helped 11–14-year-olds. No study at age 9.

grown.t: Test from memory, then check (pause and predict).
grown.note: Recalling movement sequences improved later recall (adult lab tasks). Dance Spirit's video quiz is the same idea.

grown.t: Run from the top every session, not only today's chunk.
grown.note: Practicing some figures from memory made related, unpracticed figures fade more (adults).

grown.t: Mark slowly first, then a few full-outs to prove it.
grown.note: Routines practiced by marking were rated better than ones practiced full-speed only.

grown.t: Copy details right from the start; apply teacher corrections now.
grown.note: Steps rehearsed wrong are harder to fix later; number corrections as a game, praise each one applied.

grown.t: Practice with the real track; count aloud first, then switch to musical cues.
grown.note: Tie each chunk to the music; drop the counts once secure so it doesn't look mechanical.

grown.t: Video review works best with a grown-up talking it through.
grown.note: Across 11 school studies, video plus spoken feedback beat spoken feedback alone.

grown.t: Let her choose when to watch her own clips; children need more feedback than adults.
grown.note: Children who chose when to watch learned more; reducing feedback hurt children's retention.

grown.t: Short, frequent sessions; spread across days.
grown.note: A week is very long for a 9-year-old; spreading practice over days beat one long day (adults; mixed in kids).

grown.t: Add 5–10 minutes of imagery about 3 times a week, matched to the real show.
grown.note: Imagery plus physical practice beat physical practice alone; ~10 min ×3/week worked best. Kids gained most once the skill was known.

grown.t: Perform for small audiences, film it, rehearse in costume; taper volume, keep intensity.
grown.note: Mock shows and costume runs are standard advice; sports tapers cut volume ~40–60% over ~2 weeks (adult athletes).

grown.t: Warm up before stretching; no oversplits; acro only with a spotter and mats.
grown.note: Stretching isn't a warm-up; oversplits risk ligaments; dancers who teach themselves tricks at home get hurt.

grown.t: Sleep 9–12 hours (ages 6–12); keep weekly organized hours at or under her age.
grown.note: Pediatric sleep consensus; more weekly hours than age linked to overuse injury (sports, association only).

caveat: Most motor-learning studies use adults and lab tasks; research on how children learn dance is thin. Magazine advice is expert opinion, not tested. Teachers' corrections come first.
